content:
The Loch Ness Monster never grows old, and in 2023, a huge investigation did pick up a mysterious “gloop” sound, but Nessie remained elusive. This week, the New York Post reported that someone believed they might have seen a whole family of the elusive creatures. Read on for more details.

Interesting News

Dotted among pickle snacks, Disney news, and an alarming story about how 1.3 billion humans will end up in a terrible way if Yellowstone’s supervolcano erupts, was a story about Scotland’s Loch Ness monster.

What makes people stop and click the mystery? Probably, it’s our insatiable demand for the unexplained. Of course, if it becomes explained, many people might wander off annoyed.

A Serious Report

Seriously though, the outlet reported that “Julie Fraser made the discovery of the three mysterious figures from space last week, and has reported the images to The Official Loch Ness Sightings Register.”

Yes folks, it’s a real image of not just one Nessie but a whole family of them, and they looked suspiciously like whales.

Fraser had a reason for ruling out boats. She noted there was “no V-shaped wake behind the three objects, unlike a pleasure boat visible nearby.”

Not to mock the report or the finder, but plenty of people noted the similarity in the shapes.

Google Earth

There were a few hopeful people, particularly because the images were discovered on “Google Earth.” And everyone knows that Google Earth can turn up some magical and fascinating images sometimes.

In this case, the Loch Ness Monster sighting came with a timestamp. The report said, “She also pointed to a 2026 timestamp embedded in the imagery, along with trees still in full leaf, as signs that the footage is recent.”

Mysteries Are Engaging 

When the outlet shared the article on Instagram, plenty of people engaged with the story. Not so much because Fraser claimed she wasn’t “a crank,” and not because she was merely Googling before an intended visit to the area. Instead, they probably engaged with it because mysterious things have always attracted human curiosity.

However, hundreds of skeptics filled the comments section. One person wrote, “All these sightings of Nessie and still not one of the Unicorns.”

Here are a few more responses from the discussion that followed:

  • “Let’s zoom in on these blurs to make them larger more distorted blurs.”
  • “What will eat us first? AI or Loch Ness Monster?”
  • “The Lochness Monster was debunked DECADES ago. Literally!”
  • I’m not sure that’s blurry enough to be nessie.”
  • Clearly that is Big Foot, his wife and kid sailing across the lake. Nothing magical about this.”

And someone with an AI-themed account, @support_artificialintelligence, advised with all seriousness, “Loch Ness is a great reminder that curiosity and skepticism can exist at the same time.” It added, rather obviously, “A mysterious image is worth investigating, but calling something “unexplained” is very different from proving what it is.”

A Bigger Mystery?

But the AI reply produced perhaps the greatest mystery in the entire story. Why on earth did an AI detector not detect the obviously AI-generated comment?

There’s actually a whole new field of science popping up for writers that might be way more interesting than possible waves, submarines, or whales infesting Loch Ness.

What are your thoughts? Join the discussion and then come back for all your interesting news and updates.
